quotes.quote: Cherax holthuisi is a crayfish endemic to West Papua, Indonesia.
It is found only in Lake Aitinjo on the Bird's Head Peninsula at the western end of New Guinea, in the Indonesian province of West Papua.

sections.html:
• Name: Orange crayfish
  • Other names: Apricot crayfish, Apricot cherax, Orange Papua New Guinea crayfish
  • Minimum tank size: 60 litres
  • Breeding: easy to medium
  • Diet: omnivore
  • Temperament: conditionally peaceful
  • Life span: up to 7 years
  • Colour forms: besides the orange ones there are also grey, whitish, yellow or bluish individuals

Cherax holthuisi is a crayfish endemic to West Papua, Indonesia. It is found only in Lake Aitinjo on the Bird's Head Peninsula at the western end of New Guinea, in the Indonesian province of West Papua.

The lake is relatively small, only 4 kilometres long and up to 350 metres wide, and is surrounded by steep mountains. Cherax holthuisi lives underground rather than in the open. In nature, this species is found in dense aquatic vegetation.

Too many Cherax holthuisi in insufficient space can easily lead to health problems, increased aggression, and cannibalism. Overcrowding is the main source of stress for crayfish, particularly when there is more than one male, as males are more aggressive than females.

The minimum recommended tank size for one Orange crayfish is 40 litres. A pair (male and female) requires at least 60 litres. A larger tank is always preferable for the stability of water chemistry and makes it easier to create diverse hiding areas.

Long tanks are better than tall tanks of the same size, since crayfish mostly need a place to crawl from side to side, not up and down.

Crayfish are very good escape artists. It is absolutely necessary to cover the tank, and they are strong enough to move the lid, so make sure it is stable.

Keeping Orange crayfish is not very difficult because they have no strict water quality requirements. Before bringing them home, make sure the tank is properly cycled and filtration works as it should; no ammonia or nitrites should be detectable.

  • Temperature: 22–24 °C.
  • pH: 7.0–8.0, although slightly acidic water (pH 6.5) is not a problem.
  • Hardness: KH 1–6 and GH 3–12.
  • Maintenance: 20–25% water changes every week.

These crayfish can live in tap water, but it must be prepared first. Age the water for a few days to remove chlorine. Ageing does not remove chloramines; if your city water contains them, use a water conditioner to neutralise them.

Regardless of their hardiness, acclimate crayfish before putting them into the tank.

Filtration: no special requirements, as long as the filter suits the tank size. Adult Orange crayfish may chip and chew on a sponge filter; to avoid this, use a hang-on-back or canister filter.

Oxygen: oxygen is also required in the water and can be provided with an additional pump apart from the filter.

Lighting: no special requirements. In the wild they are nocturnal and live with very little light. If the tank has plants or other animals, adapt the lighting to their needs.

Substrate: small gravel and/or sand that they can burrow into is ideal, and also makes the substrate easier to clean after feeding.

Decorations and hiding spots: shelter is a key requirement for any crayfish. It offers protection during vulnerable periods such as moulting, protects the broodstock against predation and minimises aggression. Provide a lot of hiding places, especially in a community tank. Rocks, wood, PVC pipes and other decorations are appreciated. Crayfish prefer spots as narrow as possible for them to fit in.

Live plants: this species is not recommended for a planted tank. Orange crayfish eat and cut just about any plant, and may dig up the tank and destroy plants. The viable options are plastic plants, floating plants, or cheap plants you are ready to lose and replace.

Orange crayfish are predominantly omnivorous and detritivorous feeders. They eat whatever they can catch or find on the bottom of the tank, and decomposing organic material is an important nutrient source. In captivity, for best growth they need a good mix of meat and vegetation, with protein at about 20–30% of the diet. Crayfish may resort to cannibalism to meet protein requirements.

They will eat a wide variety of foods:

  • Blanched vegetables (broccoli, cabbage, carrots, cucumbers, lettuce, corn, spinach, peas, squash, leafy greens, etc.)
  • Fruits (apple, banana, pear, melon, mango, etc.)
  • Detritus
  • Leaf litter
  • Seeds
  • Frozen bloodworms
  • Detritus worms
  • Tubifex worms
  • Blackworms
  • Earthworms
  • Freshly crushed snails
  • Dead fish or shrimp
  • Commercial shrimp or fish food (shrimp pellets, shrimp granules, flakes, etc.)

Leaves (for example Indian almond leaves, dead beech or oak leaves) should always be on the menu, as they feed on these and need the detritus from the leaves. Supplement the diet with eggshells, cuttlebone, etc., and make sure they get enough calcium for the exoskeleton by regularly feeding specialised invertebrate foods.

Protein deficiency can hinder growth and lead to weight loss, because protein is important to maintain vital organs. Calcium is needed for several vital processes, the most obvious being the formation of the exoskeleton; calcium carbonate is the basic natural compound of the exoskeleton.

Diet type: mostly herbivorous/omnivore. Food preference: leaves and vegetables. Feeding frequency: 3–4 times a week.

Crayfish are not fast eaters. Leave their food for 12–24 hours before removing it. Leaves can be left for several days or even weeks. Remove whatever is not consumed in one day to prevent water contamination. It is better to feed at night, or at least in the evening, replicating the conditions under which they naturally eat.

Adults can be fed 3–4 times a week, whereas juveniles should be fed daily. Adjust to your livestock's requirements. Do not let them starve, or they may go after tank mates (fish, fry, etc.) or cannibalise.

Orange crayfish often drag and store food in their hiding spots; check them from time to time to prevent bacterial contamination. Do not give the same food all the time; a varied diet makes them stronger and grow faster. They become more aggressive when hungry or when they lack calcium and protein.

Fully grown Orange crayfish are one of the few types of crayfish that can be kept relatively safely in a community tank. They are not as aggressive as their cousins (blue crayfish, red crayfish, marbled crayfish, Cherax destructor, etc.), but keeping several males in a group is not recommended. Because of their big claws they move somewhat clumsily.

This species is not very active and is nocturnal. Activity peaks at dusk and gradually stops during the night, before sunrise. Once settled and without large or aggressive tank mates, they may crawl around during the day.

Like all crayfish, they are amazing climbers and will try to get out of any tank. They are a moderate burrowing species: not true diggers, but they can push out some soil to make dens. In the aquarium they can be messy and destructive, moving objects around and redecorating the aquascape.

  • Social: no
  • Active: no
  • Peaceful: yes (generally)
  • Burrowers: no (generally)

Tankmates: they are not social and may behave aggressively if threatened. Bottom-dwelling, slow-moving or long-finned fish (like bettas) will be the first to get hurt. Orange crayfish usually do not hunt dwarf shrimp, which are too small and fast, but they are opportunistic and you may still lose shrimp from time to time; keeping them together is not the best choice if you plan to breed dwarf shrimp. Ornamental snails are very likely to be caught and eaten.

Avoid keeping them with larger or aggressive fish, any other crayfish species, other freshwater crabs (with a few exceptions), and dwarf frogs. The ideal situation is a species tank.

Molting: the exoskeleton ensures protection of the internal organs but limits growth, so growth involves periodic shedding and reconstruction of the hard calcified exoskeleton. Before a molt the crayfish becomes less active, stops eating and seeks shelter; otherwise it can easily fall prey to tankmates. Never disturb a molting crayfish, and do not panic if you do not see it for a few days. Keep putting and replacing food in the tank, keep giving calcium-rich food, and do not remove the old exoskeleton, which contains lots of minerals and will be eaten later.

This species is sexually dimorphic, and the sex can be determined externally:

  • Claws: males have larger claws than females.
  • Shape: females have a wide tail; their carapace is also slightly bigger.
  • Abdomen: males have two L-shaped appendages (sperm transfer organs) behind their legs, called claspers. Females have a circular sperm receptacle between the bases of the last two pairs of walking legs.

For breeding: do not keep too many animals in too small tanks; keep a male-to-female ratio of 1:1; provide enough high-quality food; give many hiding places (juveniles especially need numerous shelters); ensure proper water quality with a sufficiently high oxygen level.

Mating: if a female is ready, she allows a male to approach. The male flips the female over, clamps her claws, and deposits spermatophores in a protective receptacle in the female. The female then folds her tail over, placing the spermatophores under her body so she can fertilise her eggs. If females are not ready to mate, they will always escape even when the males are bigger and stronger.

Eggs: the number of eggs varies with female size and water temperature; large females can carry more eggs. Females usually carry a few dozen eggs and use their pleopods to keep them clean and well-oxygenated. Depending on temperature, hatching usually takes 4–6 weeks.

Hatching: Cherax holthuisi has direct development, with no larval stages or metamorphosis. Newly hatched young cannot live separately from the mother for the first several days and molt a few times before becoming independent. After separation from the mother, keep the babies in a rearing tank to prevent aggression from adults.

In 1952, Dutch ichthyologist Dr. Marinus Boeseman collected 9 specimens of genus Cherax from locals on the shores of Lake Aitinjo. These unknown specimens were deposited in the Rijksmuseum van Natuurlijke Historie as lots RMNH D 51503 and RMNH D 51504.

In 2006, German carcinologists Reinhard Pekny and Christian Lukhaup attempted to identify some exotic crayfish on the pet market in Germany. Their specimens matched Boeseman's undescribed specimens. The new species was named Cherax holthuisi in honor of Lipke Holthuis.

Orange crayfish are not large animals. Generally, they grow only up to 8–10 cm long. They are available in bright-coloured morphs such as pink, orange, or pale yellow. Blue, grey, and whitish strains also exist in the aquarium trade due to selective breeding; these come from captive breeding, and there is no information on who, how, when, and where they first originated.

It can be hard to tell Cherax holthuisi, Cherax snowden (Orange Tip crayfish) and Cherax subterigneus (Black Orange Tip crayfish) apart, especially when young. Cherax holthuisi is mainly differentiated by the form of the rostrum, the shape of the claws, and the small size of its eyes. Its rostrum has 2 indentations on each side and several indistinct lobes, with no spines; the tips of the chelae are striking orange; the main colour is yellow. C. snowden has 2 rostral teeth on each side near the apex and broader, longer claws, with a dark green to light green or greenish-grey main colour. In C. subterigneus the rostrum is 1.8–2.1 times as long as its basal width (1.5 times in the Orange crayfish), and the main colour is dark yellowish.

Currently, there is no data on the maximum lifespan in the wild. In captivity, Orange crayfish can live up to 5–7 years if appropriately cared for.

Because Cherax holthuisi is heavily exploited for ornamental purposes, it was included in the IUCN Red List of Threatened Species.

• Lukhaup, C., and R. Pekny. “Cherax (Cherax) holthuisi, a new species of crayfish (Crustacea: Decapoda: Parastacidae) from the centre of the Vogelkop Peninsula in Irian Jaya (West New Guinea), Indonesia.” Zoologische Mededelingen 80, no. 1 (2006): 101-107.
